title: Stagewise data attribution: does the influence-dynamics phase-transition story replicate on a tiny model?

original_idea.body:
# Stagewise data attribution: does the influence-dynamics phase-transition story replicate on a tiny model?

**Problem:** Influence Dynamics and Stagewise Data Attribution (arXiv:2510.12071) connects SLT phase transitions to how training data's influence shifts in stages — a surprising bridge between developmental interpretability and data attribution. Being recent and from one group, whether the stagewise influence-shift replicates on an independent small task is open.

**Direction:** Train a small model on a task with a known phase transition (grokking or list-sorting), checkpointing throughout. Use a cheap influence proxy (e.g. TracIn-style gradient-dot-product influence) on a small probe set and measure whether the most influential training examples change abruptly around the phase transition, as the theory predicts. Compare influence-shift timing to the loss-curve transition.

**Why it matters:** If which data 'matters' shifts sharply at developmental phase transitions, this gives a tool for understanding when alignment-relevant behaviors get locked in — and from which data. Independent small-scale replication is feasible in 30h on one GPU with open methods.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:2510.12071 (influence dynamics / stagewise data attribution) and the SLT/devinterp line (arXiv:2410.02984). Context open problem: inductive biases / structure formation.

title: Probing across layers: where in a small model is 'truth' most linearly recoverable, and does it move with deception?

original_idea.body:
# Probing across layers: where in a small model is 'truth' most linearly recoverable, and does it move with deception?

**Problem:** The ELK probing line found that linear probes recover a model's knowledge independently of its output 'especially in middle layers.' Whether this middle-layer truth locus shifts when a model is induced to be deceptive — and how stable the locus is across tasks — is a sharp, accessible follow-up.

**Direction:** On a small open model, train per-layer linear truth probes on a QA set and chart truth-recovery AUROC by layer to reproduce the middle-layer peak. Then induce deceptive behavior (a quirky/lying persona) and re-measure the per-layer profile, testing whether the truth signal moves, weakens, or stays put. Repeat across two or three task domains to assess locus stability.

**Why it matters:** Knowing where and how stably truth is encoded — and whether deception relocates it — is foundational for ELK and for building reliable monitors. A clean layerwise study is ideal beginner work, open models on one GPU, no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in the ELK probing finding that middle-layer linear probes recover truth (arXiv:2212.03827, arXiv:2312.01037). Context open problem: formal ELK frameworks.

title: Testing whether prover-estimator debate evades obfuscated arguments on a constructed hard instance

# Testing whether prover-estimator debate evades obfuscated arguments on a constructed hard instance

**Problem:** Prover-estimator debate (arXiv:2506.13609) is proposed to evade the obfuscated-arguments problem, where a dishonest prover cheaply produces an argument the honest prover needs exponential effort to refute. The protocol's advantage is mostly theoretical; a small constructed test of whether it beats plain debate on a deliberately obfuscatable task is open.

**Direction:** Build a tiny task with a decomposable claim where a dishonest answer can be 'obfuscated' (split into many individually-plausible-looking sub-steps, one of which is wrong). Implement plain LLM debate and a simplified prover-estimator variant (where the estimator assigns probabilities to sub-claims) using small open models, and measure judge accuracy at catching the planted error under each protocol as the number of obfuscating sub-steps grows.

**Why it matters:** Whether new debate protocols actually defeat obfuscated arguments determines if debate can be a sound scalable-oversight mechanism. A small constructed-instance test is high counterfactual value and runs on open models / one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Grounded in arXiv:2506.13609 (prover-estimator debate / obfuscated arguments) and arXiv:2311.14125 (doubly-efficient debate). Methodology: game theory, scalable oversight.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable (judge accuracy vs obfuscation depth under two protocols) though protocol implementation is nontrivial.

title: Replicating the ELK 'quirky models' truth probe on a model family it was never tested on

# Replicating the ELK 'quirky models' truth probe on a model family it was never tested on

**Problem:** The Eliciting Latent Knowledge work showed that a linear probe on middle-layer activations of LoRA-finetuned 'quirky' models recovers ~89% of the AUROC gap between truthful and untruthful contexts. But the original quirky-models suite was built on a specific set of base models; it is unclear whether the linear-truth-probe result transfers to a different open model family (e.g., Qwen2.5 vs. the original Pythia/Llama lineage).

**Direction:** Take the EleutherAI elk-generalization datasets and probing code. Instead of training new quirky models, reproduce the *probing* pipeline: extract activations from an already-released quirky model and an off-the-shelf small instruct model of a different family, train logistic-regression-on-contrast-pairs probes, and measure how much of the truthful/untruthful AUROC gap is recovered. Report per-layer probe accuracy curves and compare to the published ~89% number.

**Why it matters:** ELK is a core unsolved formal-alignment problem (ARC's agenda). If a cheap linear probe robustly elicits a model's latent 'knows the true answer' signal even when the model lies, that is a building block for scalable oversight. Testing transfer across model families tells us whether the result is a quirk of one lineage or a general property of how transformers store truth — directly relevant to whether ELK-style probes could ever be deployed.

**Relevant context:** Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models (arXiv:2312.01037): linear probe recovers 89% of AUROC gap, 75% on harder questions; mechanistic anomaly detector hits 0.95 AUROC. EleutherAI/elk-generalization repo provides 12 datasets and code. Open Problem (context): 'Develop formal frameworks for eliciting latent knowledge (ELK)'.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Clear inherited methodology (existing repo + datasets, reuse released models, no training) executable by novice+mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (per-layer probe curves on a new family vs published ~89%) with few dependencies.

title: Does the 'geometry of truth' linear structure survive on non-English statements?

original_idea.body:
# Does the 'geometry of truth' linear structure survive on non-English statements?

**Problem:** Marks & Tegmark's 'Geometry of Truth' found an emergent linear true/false direction in LLM representations, with difference-in-mean probes generalizing across English datasets and causally steering outputs. It is an open question whether this linear structure exists and transfers when the same factual statements are presented in another language.

**Direction:** Replicate the difference-in-mean truth probe on a small open model, but translate the original true/false datasets into 2-3 other languages (using a translation API or existing parallel datasets). Train the probe on English, test cross-lingually, and vice versa. Report whether a single shared truth direction exists across languages or whether each language has its own. Visualize with PCA exactly as the original paper did.

**Why it matters:** If truth is represented along a *language-independent* direction, that strengthens the case that probes capture a genuine semantic 'is-this-true' feature rather than surface statistics — important for ELK and for trusting probes as monitors. A monolingual truth direction would be a warning that probe-based oversight has multilingual blind spots, a concern for global deployment that frontier labs under-prioritize.

**Relevant context:** The Geometry of Truth (arXiv:2310.06824): emergent linear true/false structure, difference-in-mean probes generalize and are causally implicated; follow-up arXiv:2506.00823 studies consistency/generalization across logical transformations. Common Methodologies (context): linear-algebraic probing of representations.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain (cross-lingual truth direction informs probe-based honesty monitoring) but the link to catastrophic-risk reduction has a gap.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Standard difference-in-mean probing + translation, public datasets/models; beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (cross-lingual truth-direction transfer) with few dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: public models, multilingual blind-spot concern labs under-prioritize.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Multilingual representation work exists; whether the geometry-of-truth direction transfers cross-lingually is plausibly open.

title: Reproducing grokking on a different algebraic structure than modular addition

original_idea.body:
# Reproducing grokking on a different algebraic structure than modular addition

**Problem:** Grokking (delayed generalization) was discovered on small transformers learning modular arithmetic, and 'Progress measures for grokking' explained modular addition via a Fourier circuit. Most replications stick to modular addition with P=113. It is unclear how robustly grokking and its phase-transition signature appear on a *structurally different* algebraic task (e.g., a non-abelian group operation like permutation composition, or a finite-field multiplication).

**Direction:** Train a tiny 1-2 layer transformer (trainable in minutes on a consumer GPU) on a non-modular-addition algebraic task. Reproduce the canonical grokking curves (train acc spikes early, val acc grokks late), measure the data-fraction threshold for grokking, and compare the timing/sharpness of the generalization phase transition to published modular-addition results.

**Why it matters:** Grokking is a model organism for sudden capability emergence — a phenomenon with direct safety relevance (capabilities can appear abruptly long after training loss looks stable). Characterizing whether and when grokking generalizes to different task structures helps build a science of emergence that is hard to do at the frontier but easy on toy models, and needs no proprietary data or lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Grokking (arXiv:2201.02177); Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability (arXiv:2301.05217); modular addition P=113 grokks for many data fractions; arXiv:2402.16726 shows subtraction/multiplication have different circuit dynamics. Recent Surprising Results (context): gap between theoretical and empirical alignment progress invites empirical follow-ups.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Tiny transformer on a synthetic task, minutes of compute; highly accessible to beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused single-experiment deliverable (reproduce grokking curves on a new algebraic task).

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Doable externally but grokking on varied algebraic tasks is already a crowded toy-model area; mixed counterfactual value.

# Re-running the weight-initialization-and-grokking study with a different optimizer

**Problem:** A recent study found weight initialization (e.g., Xavier) strongly affects whether and how fast small transformers grok arithmetic over finite fields. That study held the optimizer roughly fixed. The interaction between *optimizer choice* (and weight decay) and grokking onset is less systematically mapped, despite weight decay being central to the grokking story.

**Direction:** Reproduce the init-sweep grokking experiment but vary the optimizer (AdamW vs. SGD-momentum vs. Adam with different weight-decay coefficients) on the same finite-field arithmetic tasks. Use the published checklist-style protocol (exact dataset cardinalities, seeds, hyperparameters) so results are directly comparable. Report grokking-onset epoch as a function of (init x optimizer x weight-decay).

**Why it matters:** Understanding which training-dynamics knobs control delayed generalization sharpens our theory of when hidden capabilities crystallize. This is a clean, fully-reproducible inductive-bias study (an explicit open problem: 'theoretical study of inductive biases and their implications for alignment') that requires only minutes of consumer-GPU compute per run and no large datasets.

**Relevant context:** Sakana 'unlocking grokking' weight-initialization study (controlled finite-field arithmetic, checklist protocol, Xavier best for convergence). # Testing whether neural scaling laws hold in the sub-1M-parameter 'tiny' regime on a safety-relevant task

**Problem:** Kaplan-style scaling laws (loss ~ power law in model size) were established over many orders of magnitude, but the far-left, tiny end of the curve (<~20M params) is under-characterized; recent work asks whether the same power law even extends there. No one has checked whether the tiny-regime scaling shape holds for a *safety-flavored* objective like a toxicity/refusal classifier rather than generic language modeling.

**Direction:** Train a ladder of very small models (a few thousand to ~1M params) on a fixed small classification task (e.g., predicting whether a short text is a harmful request, using an existing labeled dataset). Each run is seconds-to-minutes. Fit a power law to test-loss vs. model size and vs. data size, and report whether the tiny regime matches the canonical exponent or deviates.

**Why it matters:** Scaling laws underpin frontier-safety forecasting (predicting capabilities before training). Knowing whether they hold and with what exponent for safety-relevant objectives in regimes anyone can train tells us how trustworthy extrapolation is. It is pure counterfactual-value work: no large models, no lab compute, just a clean reproducible curve.

**Relevant context:** Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (arXiv:2001.08361), alpha~0.076 for LM loss; 'Scaling Laws in the Tiny Regime' (arXiv:2603.07365) notes the <20M-param regime is poorly understood; nanoGPT scaling-law replication repo exists. title: Replicating reward-model overoptimization (Goodhart) curves on a hand-built toy proxy

original_idea.body:
# Replicating reward-model overoptimization (Goodhart) curves on a hand-built toy proxy

**Problem:** Gao et al. found scaling laws for reward-model overoptimization: optimizing a proxy reward past a critical point degrades the true ('gold') reward, following a predictable functional form. The full study used large RLHF setups. A faithful small replication of the *shape* of these overoptimization curves in a controllable toy setting, where the gold reward is known exactly, would make the phenomenon teachable and let us test which Goodhart 'type' dominates.

**Direction:** Build a tiny RL/bandit or best-of-n toy where the gold reward is a known function and the proxy is gold-plus-noise (the simplest regressional-Goodhart construction). Vary optimization pressure (KL budget / best-of-n N) and reproduce the rise-then-fall of gold reward vs. proxy reward. Then add a deliberately *miscausal* proxy to elicit causal/extremal Goodhart and compare curve shapes.

**Why it matters:** Reward hacking via proxy overoptimization is a central, long-horizon alignment threat. A clean, reproducible toy that reproduces the published overoptimization functional form — and dissects which of Garrabrant's four Goodhart types is operative — gives the community a no-lab-resources testbed for studying fuzzy-reward failure, exactly the kind of diffuse problem frontier labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization (Gao et al., arXiv:2210.10760); 'Goodhart's Law in Reinforcement Learning' (OpenReview 5o9G4XF1LI) shows overoptimization across many environments; Garrabrant's four Goodhart types (Regressional/Causal/Extremal/Adversarial). Steering priority (context): fuzzy-reward / reward-hacking evaluations with no lab resources.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: reproducing reward-overoptimization curves and dissecting Goodhart types targets reward hacking, a recognized critical alignment pathway.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Bandit/best-of-n toy with a known gold reward; standard tools, beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment (rise-then-fall curve under varying optimization pressure) with clear success criteria.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected long-horizon 'gold': fuzzy-reward/reward-hacking testbed labs deprioritize, no internal access needed.

title: Replicating Toy Models of Superposition with a structured (non-uniform) feature-importance distribution

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Toy Models of Superposition with a structured (non-uniform) feature-importance distribution

**Problem:** Anthropic's Toy Models of Superposition trained tiny ReLU networks on synthetic sparse features and showed superposition emerges as a function of feature sparsity and importance. The canonical setup uses simple importance schedules. How superposition geometry (which features get dedicated dimensions vs. crammed together) changes under a *realistically skewed* feature-importance distribution (e.g., power-law / Zipfian importances) is under-explored.

**Direction:** Reproduce the toy-superposition model exactly (it trains in seconds), then replace the feature-importance vector with a Zipfian distribution and sweep sparsity. Measure how many features get 'pulled out' of superposition, the geometry (digons/pentagons/etc. from the original paper), and interference, comparing against the uniform-importance baseline figures.

**Why it matters:** Superposition is why neurons are polysemantic, which is the central obstacle to mechanistic interpretability and to the open problem of 'formal mechanistic explanations of neural network behaviors.' Real feature importances are heavy-tailed, so checking whether the published superposition phenomenology survives skewed importances tells us how well toy-model intuitions transfer to real networks — fully reproducible on a CPU/GPU laptop.

**Relevant context:** Toy Models of Superposition (Anthropic, transformer-circuits.pub 2022; arXiv:2209.10652): superposition as function of sparsity/importance, geometric configurations. Open Problem (context): 'formal mechanistic explanations of neural network behaviors for identifying anomalous behavior on novel inputs'.

title: Can an L1 sparse autoencoder recover ground-truth features under correlated toy features?

original_idea.body:
# Can an L1 sparse autoencoder recover ground-truth features under correlated (non-independent) toy features?

**Problem:** On small toy models, a single-layer L1 autoencoder can recover the ground-truth sparse features that generated the data, but later work showed SAEs can instead find *composed* features due to the L1 penalty. A clean question: how does feature recovery degrade as the toy features become correlated rather than independent — the realistic case?

**Direction:** Reproduce the toy-model + L1-SAE pipeline. Generate synthetic data with independent sparse features (baseline, reproduce ground-truth recovery), then introduce controlled pairwise correlations between features and measure how recovery quality (e.g., max cosine sim to true features, number of composed/ghost features) degrades. Report the correlation threshold at which the SAE starts hallucinating composed features.

**Why it matters:** SAEs are the leading tool for decomposing models into interpretable features, central to the 'formal mechanistic explanations' open problem. Knowing exactly when they fail (correlated features) on ground-truth-known toys is a counterfactually valuable contribution: it stress-tests an interpretability method's assumptions without needing any frontier model or lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic Toy Models of Superposition + 'Sparse autoencoders find composed features in small toy models' (Evan Anders / LessWrong, 2024): L1 penalty causes composed-feature recovery; single-layer autoencoder can recover ground-truth features in the simplest case. Open Problem (context): mechanistic explanations of NN behavior.

title: Reproducing the induction-head phase transition and checking its timing on a different tokenizer/data

# Reproducing the induction-head phase transition and checking its timing on a different tokenizer/data

**Problem:** Two-layer transformers develop induction heads at a sharp phase transition that coincides with a bump in the loss curve and the onset of in-context learning. The canonical demonstrations use specific synthetic Markov data or particular corpora. Whether the *timing and sharpness* of the induction-head phase transition is robust to a different data-generating process (e.g., higher-order Markov chains, or a different tokenization granularity) is not well-mapped.

Detect the induction head via the standard prefix-matching attention pattern, and report how transition timing shifts. Compare to the published 'abrupt emergence' picture.

**Why it matters:** Induction heads are the cleanest known case of an abrupt, mechanistically-understood capability emergence — a model organism for emergent in-context learning. Characterizing how robust the emergence is to data structure deepens the empirical science of phase transitions in training, which underlies forecasting of surprising capability jumps, and is doable entirely on toy models with no proprietary resources.

**Relevant context:** Induction-head literature: phase transition coincides with ICL onset and a loss bump; 'On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning' (arXiv:2511.01033) and 'Two-Layer Transformers Provably Represent Induction Heads on Any-Order Markov Chains' (arXiv:2508.07208). # Replicating RLHF-worsens-calibration on small open instruct models vs. their base versions

**Problem:** It has been reported (e.g., for GPT-4) that RLHF can worsen a model's calibration relative to its pretrained base, and that RLHF models over-report high verbalized confidence. This has mostly been studied on proprietary frontier models. Whether the same calibration degradation appears between a *small open base model and its open RLHF/instruct-tuned sibling* (where we can inspect both) is testable but underexplored.

**Direction:** Take an open base model and its instruct/RLHF-tuned counterpart of the same size (e.g., a base vs. instruct pair). On a multiple-choice QA benchmark, compare (a) token-probability calibration and (b) verbalized-confidence calibration via expected calibration error and reliability diagrams. Replicate the published direction-of-effect (RLHF worsens calibration) on a model where both checkpoints are public.

**Why it matters:** Calibrated uncertainty is a safety-critical property: an overconfident model that won't say 'I don't know' is dangerous in high-stakes use. Confirming whether the RLHF-calibration-degradation finding generalizes to inspectable open model pairs — rather than just closed frontier models — is high counterfactual value and gives a reproducible measurement anyone can extend.

**Relevant context:** 'Just Ask for Calibration' (arXiv:2305.14975): RLHF worsens conditional-probability calibration, verbalized confidence can recover it; surveys note RLHF models emit 80-100% confidence with ECE up to 0.30+. Steering priority (context): evaluations needing no lab resources; safety relevance of honesty/uncertainty.
